matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

This behavior is rare in the npm ecosystem and is commonly exploited by malware.

attack_chain.action: User installs or updates a dependency (e.g., styled-components@5.3.5) that introduces a postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution during installation.

attack_chain.action: Telemetry-collecting dependency (e.g., @scarf/scarf via angular-calendar) is imported, sending usage data to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential exfiltration of environment or usage data.

attack_chain.action: Native code dependency (e.g., deasync) is loaded, executing unauditable binary code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for hidden malicious payloads or privilege escalation.

attack_chain.action: Troll or parody package (e.g., bowserify) injects unwanted assets and code into application bundles.
attack_chain.leads_to: Polluted or altered application behavior, user confusion.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of install or postinstall scripts in package.json (scripts.install/postinstall) that execute external files or commands
Network requests to known telemetry or tracking domains (e.g., scarf.sh) at import-time or runtime
Loading of native binary modules (.node files) in JavaScript packages during import or execution
Injection of non-standard assets (e.g., images) or code into bundles by dependencies
Package names that closely resemble or parody popular packages (typosquatting/parody)
file_indicators: package.json with install or postinstall scripts referencing external files
node_modules/**/build/Release/*.node
node_modules/@scarf/scarf/**
node_modules/bowserify/**
Unexpected image or asset files (e.g., bowser.png) in application bundles
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS requests to scarf.sh/track
Any network request during install or import-time to unknown or unapproved domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified install/postinstall scripts in package.json during dependency updates. Flag packages that load native binaries (.node files) or make network requests at import-time or runtime. Detect dependencies that inject unexpected assets or code into application bundles. Identify package names that closely resemble popular packages (typosquats or parodies). Alert on outbound network connections to known telemetry or tracking domains from dependencies, especially during installation or import-time.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of ---js front matter blocks in Markdown input
Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing
Direct filesystem access via require('fs').readFileSync in user-supplied content
Injection of sensitive file contents into user-facing output (PDF)
Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits specially crafted Markdown containing a ---js front matter block with malicious JavaScript to the invoice generator.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.action: The code injects the flag value into the CSS of the generated PDF document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript during Markdown-to-PDF conversion
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /flag.txt) from within Markdown processing
User-controlled input leading to server-side code execution during document generation
file_indicators: Markdown files or input containing ---js front matter blocks
References to require('fs') or other Node.js modules in user-supplied Markdown content
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections initiated during Markdown processing (if exfiltration is attempted via network)
No direct network indicators in this specific exploit, but possible in variants where exfiltration is performed over the network
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
let a = $.extend(true, {}, JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"devMode": true}}'));
console.log({}.devMode); // true
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs a deep merge using jQuery.extend(true, ...) with user-controlled input containing a __proto__ property, resulting in the devMode property being set on Object.prototype and making it globally accessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user input to modify the Object prototype, which can introduce attacker-controlled properties globally and compromise application logic or security boundaries.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, deep merging should only affect the target object, not the global prototype chain. Here, untrusted input is able to pollute the prototype, impacting all objects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deep merging of configuration objects is common, but should never allow modification of the prototype chain.
key_indicators: Use of __proto__ property in user input
Recursive merge without filtering prototype keys
Global side effects such as {}.devMode === true

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of jQuery allow prototype pollution via the extend() API. Attackers can inject properties into the Object prototype by supplying objects with __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys as input to deep merge operations. This enables privilege escalation, denial of service, or arbitrary code path manipulation in applications that use jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted input, as malicious properties become globally accessible on all objects.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits user-controlled JSON or object containing a __proto__ property.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the input using unsafe deep merge or mapping.

attack_chain.action: Application merges or assigns the user input into an object using jQuery.extend() or direct assignment, without filtering prototype keys.
attack_chain.leads_to: The Object prototype is polluted with attacker-controlled properties.

attack_chain.action: Subsequent code accesses properties (e.g., isAdmin, toString) on objects, which now resolve to attacker-controlled values via the prototype chain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation, logic manipulation, or denial of service.

behavioral_signatures: Deep merge operations (e.g., jQuery.extend(true, ...)) involving user-controlled objects containing __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys
Assignment to object properties using user-controlled keys without filtering for prototype pollution vectors
Unexpected global properties or methods (e.g., isAdmin, toString) appearing on Object.prototype at runtime
file_indicators: Use of jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted or user-supplied input
Direct assignment to ["__proto__"], ["constructor"], or ["prototype"] in application code
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deep merge or object assignment operations where user-controlled data is used as keys, especially if the keys are __proto__, prototype, or constructor. Audit code for use of jQuery.extend(true, ...) or similar recursive merge utilities with untrusted input. Use static analysis to flag assignments to __proto__ or suspicious object key usage. At runtime, detect unexpected properties or methods on Object.prototype or global objects, such as isAdmin or toString, that are not part of the application's intended logic.

Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. This results in a Denial of Service (DoS) condition by overwhelming the user's system with excessive network and disk activity, and also locks the npm registry by making it impossible for developers to remove their own packages due to dependency entanglement. matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs a deep merge using jQuery.extend(true, ...) with user-controlled input containing a __proto__ property, resulting in the devMode property being set on Object.prototype and making it globally accessible.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows user input to modify the Object prototype, which can introduce attacker-controlled properties globally and compromise application logic or security boundaries.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, deep merging should only affect the target object, not the global prototype chain. Here, untrusted input is able to pollute the prototype, impacting all objects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deep merging of configuration objects is common, but should never allow modification of the prototype chain.
key_indicators: Use of __proto__ property in user input
Recursive merge without filtering prototype keys
Global side effects such as {}.devMode === true

package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of jQuery allow prototype pollution via the extend() API. Attackers can inject properties into the Object prototype by supplying objects with __proto__, constructor, or prototype keys as input to deep merge operations. This enables privilege escalation, denial of service, or arbitrary code path manipulation in applications that use jQuery.extend(true, ...) with untrusted input, as malicious properties become globally accessible on all objects.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits user-controlled JSON or object containing a __proto__ property.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application processes the input using unsafe deep merge or mapping.

attack_chain.action: Application merges or assigns the user input into an object using jQuery.extend() or direct assignment, without filtering prototype keys.
attack_chain.leads_to: The Object prototype is polluted with attacker-controlled properties.

attack_chain.action: Subsequent code accesses properties (e.g., isAdmin, toString) on objects, which now resolve to attacker-controlled values via the prototype chain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation, logic manipulation, or denial of service.

Assignment to object properties using user-controlled keys without filtering for prototype pollution vectors
Unexpected global properties or methods (e.g., isAdmin, toString) appearing on Object.prototype at runtime

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At application startup, the Electron app sets contextIsolation to false in the webPreferences, which allows JavaScript running in the renderer process to directly access NodeJS APIs, removing the security boundary and enabling untrusted web content to interact with system-level resources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling context isolation exposes powerful NodeJS APIs to all web content loaded in the renderer, allowing any JavaScript (including from third-party or untrusted sources) to execute system commands or access the filesystem.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Electron apps are expected to enforce context isolation to prevent web content from accessing NodeJS APIs. Disabling this protection breaks the security model and exposes the host system to code execution from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legacy Electron apps may disable context isolation for compatibility with older codebases, but this practice is strongly discouraged and considered insecure.

NodeJS APIs accessible from renderer process JavaScript

package_info.why_malicious: The Electron framework, as used in Discord, was configured insecurely with contextIsolation set to false, which allowed web content to directly access NodeJS APIs. This misconfiguration, combined with a framebusting vulnerability and an XSS on a third-party site (SketchFab), enabled attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE) on user machines. While Electron itself is not intentionally malicious, these vulnerabilities and insecure configurations in the affected versions allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code, making the package as used in this context effectively malicious.

attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code now runs in the main Electron renderer context, bypassing intended isolation.

attack_chain.action: Due to contextIsolation: false, malicious JavaScript gains access to NodeJS APIs and executes arbitrary system commands via child_process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the user's machine, achieving the attacker's objective.

Compared to the known malicious patterns, this code lacks any suspicious API usage such as require('fs'), dynamic code execution, or bundle manipulation. The behavior is consistent with legitimate styling logic and development warnings, which are common in frontend or rendering libraries.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

package_info.why_malicious: Version 5.3.5 of styled-components introduced a postinstall script (protestware) that executes arbitrary code during installation. While the specific script in this case is not overtly malicious, the addition of an install script in a widely used package is highly unusual and creates a significant risk vector, as it allows for arbitrary code execution on user systems during package installation. This behavior is rare in the npm ecosystem and is commonly exploited by malware.

attack_chain.action: User installs or updates a dependency (e.g., styled-components@5.3.5) that introduces a postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution during installation.

attack_chain.leads_to: Potential exfiltration of environment or usage data.

attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for hidden malicious payloads or privilege escalation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code sets the NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED environment variable to '0', globally disabling TLS certificate validation for all subsequent HTTPS requests, resulting in the ability to communicate with servers using invalid, self-signed, or malicious certificates and exposing the system to man-in-the-middle attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling TLS certificate validation is a well-known anti-security technique that exposes all HTTPS communications to interception, tampering, and redirection to malicious servers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure applications are expected to validate TLS certificates to ensure the authenticity and integrity of communications; global overrides of this behavior are never appropriate in production code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In rare cases, developers may disable TLS validation for local testing or debugging, but this should never occur in production code or without explicit user action.
